Christmas Mocktail Recipes: 8 Festive Alcohol-Free Drinks for Your Bar, Table or Party

Bar Series • Recipes • By Nigel A. Thomas, Hospitality Executive • October 2026

Every Christmas function has guests who are not drinking alcohol: designated drivers, expectant mothers, guests who do not drink for religious or health reasons, teenagers, colleagues on early shifts. The worst thing a host or a bar can do is hand them a glass of plain juice or a can of cola while everyone else gets a proper drink. A good mocktail is built with the same care as a cocktail – balanced, cold, well garnished – and guests notice the difference.

This guide gives you eight complete Christmas mocktails with exact measures in millilitres, simple methods, four homemade syrups, and the service and costing advice I would give a hotel or restaurant team. Six are sparkling, long drinks built in the glass; two are creamy shaken coolers. All are quick enough for a busy December service. Why Mocktails Deserve a Place on the Christmas Menu

They include everyone. A table of eight at a hotel brunch often contains at least one guest who is not drinking. Offering them a proper, named, garnished drink makes them feel welcome and keeps them at the table longer.

They protect your margin. Juice, syrup and soda cost far less per serving than spirits or wine, yet a well-presented mocktail can be priced close to a cocktail. The labour is similar, the pour cost is lower, and the sale is additional rather than a replacement.

They suit the whole day. Brunch, lunch, afternoon tea, evening service and children's parties all need a festive drink. Alcohol-free options also work for corporate lunches and events where guests drive home.

They are the easiest drinks to batch. Because everything is juice, syrup and mixers, eight of these drinks can be prepared in advance with only the final top-up and garnish left for service.

Five Techniques for Better Mocktails

1. Balance sweet, sour and dilution

A great mocktail follows the same logic as a cocktail: sweetness, acidity and dilution in balance. Juices bring sweetness and some acid; lemon and lime juice sharpen; syrups add flavour and body; soda or ginger ale lengthens the drink. If a drink tastes flat, it usually needs a little more citrus. If it tastes sharp, it needs a touch more syrup or a longer top-up. Always taste before you serve.

2. Cold glass, good ice

Nothing ruins a sparkling drink faster than warm glassware or small, wet ice. Chill glasses where you can, fill them with plenty of fresh, hard ice (more ice melts more slowly), and keep all juices and mixers refrigerated. A cold drink holds its bubbles, tastes cleaner and looks better.

3. Build in order and protect the bubbles

For the sparkling drinks, add ice first, then juice and syrup, then the soda, ginger ale or ginger beer last. Pour the fizzy top-up gently down the side of the glass or over a bar spoon and stir once, lightly, from the bottom. Hard stirring knocks out the carbonation, and the drink goes flat within minutes.

4. Make your own syrups

Four of these drinks depend on flavoured syrups, and making them in-house is simple and cheap. Start from a basic simple syrup: dissolve equal parts sugar and water over low heat, then cool. For the festive flavours:

  • Rosemary syrup: steep a few fresh rosemary sprigs in the hot syrup for about 20 minutes, then strain.
  • Cinnamon syrup: simmer two or three cinnamon sticks in the syrup for 10–15 minutes, then cool and strain.
  • Gingerbread syrup: infuse the syrup with sliced fresh ginger, a cinnamon stick, a few cloves and a pinch of nutmeg; a spoonful of brown sugar or molasses gives the gingerbread depth.
  • Peppermint syrup: infuse with fresh mint leaves, or add peppermint extract a drop at a time off the heat. It is very strong, so taste as you go. Vanilla syrup follows the same method with a split vanilla pod or a little vanilla extract.

Store syrups in clean, sealed, labelled bottles in the refrigerator and use them within about a week or two. Always date the bottle, and throw out any syrup that looks cloudy or smells off. Commercial syrups are a perfectly good alternative where volume or shelf life matters.

5. Garnish with purpose

Garnish carries the Christmas theme: rosemary sprigs look like tiny trees, cinnamon sticks and orange wheels smell festive, cranberries and pomegranate seeds add colour, and crushed candy cane makes the creamy drinks look like winter. Keep garnishes fresh, dry and close to the drink, and make sure every garnish is edible or can be removed easily.

The Recipes

All recipes below make one serving. Measures are in millilitres. Always use fresh juice where possible, and use plenty of ice.

1. Cranberry Rosemary Spritz

Sparkling • Tart • Herbal

Ingredients

  • 90 ml cranberry juice
  • 20 ml lemon juice
  • 15 ml rosemary syrup
  • 90 ml soda water
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

Fresh rosemary sprig and cranberries

Method

  1. Fill a tall glass with ice.
  2. Add the cranberry juice, lemon juice and rosemary syrup.
  3. Top with soda water, stir gently and garnish.

Pro tip: Clap the rosemary sprig between your hands before you place it in the glass. That releases the aroma, so guests smell pine and herbs before they taste the drink. Use unsweetened cranberry juice if you can, as sweetened cocktail juice makes the drink too sugary.

2. Spiced Apple Fizz

Sparkling • Warm spice, cold glass

Ingredients

  • 120 ml apple juice
  • 15 ml lemon juice
  • 15 ml cinnamon syrup
  • 60 ml ginger ale
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

Thin apple slice and cinnamon stick

Method

  1. Fill a glass with ice.
  2. Add the apple juice, lemon juice and cinnamon syrup.
  3. Top with ginger ale, stir gently and garnish.

Pro tip: A cloudy, pressed apple juice tastes noticeably better than a clear, filtered one. Dip the apple slice in a little lemon juice so it does not turn brown during service.

3. Pomegranate Orange Sparkle

Sparkling • Ruby red • Bright

Ingredients

  • 90 ml pomegranate juice
  • 60 ml orange juice
  • 15 ml lime juice
  • 60 ml soda water
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

Orange slice and pomegranate seeds

Method

  1. Fill a glass with ice.
  2. Add the pomegranate, orange and lime juices.
  3. Top with soda water, stir gently and garnish.

Pro tip: Pomegranate juice is deeply coloured and slightly astringent, and the orange softens it. This is the best-looking drink on the menu in a clear glass, so choose a tall, clean glass and add the seeds last so they float at the top.

4. Gingerbread Cream Cooler

Creamy • Shaken • Dessert-style

Ingredients

  • 120 ml cold milk
  • 30 ml gingerbread syrup
  • 30 ml cream
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

A light dusting of cinnamon

Method

  1. Shake the milk, gingerbread syrup and cream with ice.
  2. Strain into a chilled glass.
  3. Dust lightly with cinnamon.

Pro tip: Shake hard for 10–12 seconds; the aeration gives a light, frothy texture. Serve it in a chilled rocks glass over fresh ice or straight up. For a dairy-free version, use oat milk and a plant-based cream, and declare the change on the menu.

5. Christmas Citrus Punch

Sparkling • Citrus • Easy to batch

Ingredients

  • 60 ml orange juice
  • 60 ml cranberry juice
  • 15 ml lemon juice
  • 60 ml ginger ale
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

Orange wheel and cinnamon stick

Method

  1. Fill a glass with ice.
  2. Add the orange, cranberry and lemon juices.
  3. Top with ginger ale, stir gently and garnish.

Pro tip: This is the best drink for a crowd. Mix the three juices in a jug ahead of time and refrigerate; at service, pour over ice and add the ginger ale. For a punch bowl, keep the ginger ale separate and add it just before guests arrive.

6. Winter Berry Mule

Sparkling • Berry • Served in a copper mug

Ingredients

  • 60 ml mixed berry purée
  • 20 ml lime juice
  • 120 ml non-alcoholic ginger beer
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

Fresh berries and lime wedge

Method

  1. Add the berry purée and lime juice to an ice-filled mug.
  2. Top with ginger beer, stir gently and garnish.

Pro tip: A copper mug holds the cold and gives the drink theatre. Make the purée in advance by blending thawed frozen berries and straining out the seeds; sweeten lightly if the berries are tart. Use a good ginger beer with real ginger heat – it is the backbone of the drink.

7. Pear Ginger Sparkler

Sparkling • Light • Golden

Ingredients

  • 100 ml pear juice
  • 15 ml lemon juice
  • 90 ml ginger ale
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

Thin pear slice

Method

  1. Fill a tall glass with ice.
  2. Add the pear juice and lemon juice.
  3. Top with ginger ale, stir gently and garnish with pear.

Pro tip: Pear is gentle and subtle, so do not overpower it. Keep the lemon at 15 ml, use a lightly flavoured ginger ale, and slice the pear paper-thin with a mandoline. Brush the slice with a little lemon juice to keep it pale.

8. Candy Cane Cooler

Creamy • Shaken • Peppermint

Ingredients

  • 120 ml cold milk
  • 20 ml peppermint syrup
  • 15 ml vanilla syrup
  • 30 ml cream
  • Ice cubes

Garnish

A little crushed candy cane

Method

  1. Shake the milk, peppermint syrup, vanilla syrup and cream with ice.
  2. Strain into a chilled glass.
  3. Sprinkle with crushed candy cane.

Pro tip: Moisten only the outer edge of the rim and dip it in the crushed candy cane for a festive rim, and sprinkle a little on top. Crush the candy cane just before service, because it absorbs moisture and turns sticky quickly. Peppermint is strong, so start with a smaller measure and adjust.

Running a Christmas Mocktail Menu

Offer a short, balanced list. Four mocktails are enough for most venues: one tart and sparkling (Cranberry Rosemary Spritz), one warm and spiced (Spiced Apple Fizz), one creamy (Gingerbread Cream Cooler) and one for a crowd (Christmas Citrus Punch). Add the others as specials or for a private function.

Batch the base, finish to order. For a function, multiply the juice and syrup portions by the number of guests, mix them in a labelled jug and refrigerate. At service, pour over ice, add the sparkling top and garnish. Do not mix the carbonated ingredients in advance. For the creamy coolers, mix the milk, cream and syrup cold, keep them refrigerated and shake to order.

Cost every drink. Cost each mocktail from the recipe including garnish, then price it so the margin is healthy. Guests will pay a fair price for a well-made festive drink, so avoid pricing it like a soft drink. Keep a standard recipe card behind the bar so every glass tastes the same.

Train the team. Run a tasting for the service staff. They should be able to describe each drink in a sentence, name the garnish and mention the allergens. A confident description turns a mocktail from an afterthought into a recommendation.

Think about children. Most of these drinks work well for children's parties, but be mindful of caffeine-free mixers, sugar levels and small garnishes. Skip rosemary sprigs and cinnamon sticks for very young guests, and make sure straws and picks are used safely.

Allergens and Safe Service

Dairy: The Gingerbread Cream Cooler and Candy Cane Cooler contain milk and cream. Always declare this on the menu and offer a dairy-free version where possible.

Other allergens. Check syrups, ginger beer and gingerbread flavourings for allergens, and note that some commercial syrups contain traces of nuts or gluten. Fruit purées can trigger allergies in some guests. Ask guests about allergies before serving.

Juice and hygiene. Use pasteurised juices for vulnerable guests, such as young children, pregnant women and the elderly. Wash fruit before garnishing, keep cut fruit refrigerated, and discard garnishes that have sat out for long. Keep dairy-based mixes cold and use them within the day.

Label clearly. Mark alcohol-free drinks on the menu and in the bar so they are never mixed up with cocktails. If a bar serves both, use separate jiggers, shakers and stirrers for mocktails, or rinse thoroughly, especially for guests who avoid alcohol for religious or health reasons.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I make these mocktails ahead for a party?

Yes, partly. Mix the juices and syrup in a jug and refrigerate for several hours, then pour over ice and add the sparkling top-up when guests arrive. For the creamy drinks, mix and chill the milk, cream and syrup and shake to order.

How long do homemade syrups last?

Stored in clean, sealed bottles in the refrigerator, simple infused syrups are best used within about one to two weeks. Label each bottle with the date, and discard any syrup that looks cloudy, smells off or shows mould.

Can I turn these into cocktails?

Many of them can. The Cranberry Rosemary Spritz, Pomegranate Orange Sparkle and Pear Ginger Sparkler all work with vodka, gin or sparkling wine, and the Winter Berry Mule is a natural base for vodka. Keep the mocktail and cocktail versions clearly labelled and separate.

What can I use instead of ginger ale?

Ginger beer gives a spicier, stronger result, and lemon-lime soda or tonic water can work for a lighter drink. Taste and adjust the citrus, as different mixers carry different sweetness.

How do I stop the drinks going flat?

Chill everything, use plenty of ice, add the carbonated mixer last, pour gently and stir only once. Open mixers just before service and do not reuse part-used bottles that have lost their fizz.
